title: Holes: squares your pawns can never guard again
outcomes: Marks the holes in one side's camp: squares in front of its pawns that none of its pawns can guard again
Names the enemy piece that could move onto a given hole
Checks that a piece can reach a hole and stay there, not only that the hole exists
Tells a hole from a square a pawn can still guard

steps.text: A **hole** is a square in front of your own pawns that none of those pawns can ever guard again, because pawns never move backward. A hole is a weakness only if an enemy piece can **reach** it and **stay** there. It is a fact about *your* pawns; your opponent decides whether it matters.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has no e-pawn and his c-pawn stands on c5, so d5 is a hole in his camp.

line.say: The knight settles on d5. No Black pawn can ever attack it, and no Black piece attacks it now.

claims.statement: No Black pawn can ever attack d5.
After Nd5 no Black piece attacks the knight.
Nd5 is among the engine's top two moves.

steps.text:
Before you call a hole a weakness, ask three things.
**Can a piece reach it?** A knight can get there in time; a bishop only squares of its colour.
**Can it stay?** If an enemy knight or bishop attacks it, it can be traded off.
**Is there something to aim at from there?**
This is a *rule of thumb*: the more answers are yes, the more the hole matters.

steps.title: The same hole, one piece different
steps.prompt: In the first two positions only one Black piece differs (a knight on b8 or on d7), and White's knight can go to c5. Predict, then check: is Nc5 a good move in each? The third position asks a different question: is the square a hole at all?
In the last position, which of the three questions (reach, stay, aim) did you ask first, and which did you skip? Write one line.
